turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mrs Hale. I'll just do your weight and blood pressure before Dr Shah comes through.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, thank you. Sorry if I'm flustered, the bus was late and I've been fretting about this all weekend.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're alright, take your time. Step on the scales. That's 86.5 kilograms. Blood pressure is 146 over 84, and your pulse is 72.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): 86.5, is that bad? I knew I'd put a bit on since I stopped walking. Is 146 dangerous? I do take my blood pressure tablet, every morning, I never miss it.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been googling, that's the trouble. I'm Lauren, her daughter. I came so she wouldn't forget half of it.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Nice to meet you. While I've got the list up, it says diclofenac tablets, 50 milligrams. Is that what you take?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's wrong. I get the 25 milligram ones from the chemist, and only sometimes, about twice a week when the knee is really grumbling. I don't take 50.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm not getting in the middle of the boxes. Mum, tell them about the gel as well when the doctor comes.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): I'll leave that dose for Dr Shah to untangle. He won't be a minute. There's water on the side if you want it.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Lauren, did you lock the car? I keep thinking I didn't.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's locked. Sit down, Mum.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mrs Hale, I'm Dr Shah. And you've got someone with you.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Lauren, her daughter. I'll chip in if she misses something, if that's alright.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Of course. What's brought you in? Start wherever feels easiest.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my right knee. For about four months it's hurt going down the stairs, nearly every time, and at night a deep ache wakes me two or three nights a week. I keep panicking it's something awful.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can hear you're worried, and we'll go through it properly. Nothing you've said so far sounds like an emergency. When did this start?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about four months ago. After Christmas it was a niggle, and then it just stayed. Well, actually, maybe it was a bit before, but I'll say four months.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She gave up the Tuesday walking group. That's when I noticed, because she stopped coming round on the way home.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Going down the stairs, is that every time, or only on bad days?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Nearly every time, yes. Coming up is easier, which is weird, isn't it? Why would down be worse? Is that a bad sign?
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's actually very common with knee joint pain, so I wouldn't read disaster into it. And at night, what is that like?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Same deep ache, inside the knee. I lie there thinking about it, which only makes me more wound up. Sorry, I'm jumping about.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the knee lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No locking, and it hasn't given way. I'm just slow and careful, I hold the rail. I'm 74, I feel about 90 on the stairs.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling you've noticed, or does the knee feel hot?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit puffy by the evening, some days. Not hot. I checked, because I read about infection and that frightened me.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the other knee, or the hips?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Left knee is fine. Hips are fine. My lower back aches if I've been sitting too long, but that's been years, it's not why I'm here.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, I'm talking too much. Do you need me to stop?
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not at all, this is useful. What are you actually putting on the knee, or taking?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac gel, morning and night, rubbed into the right knee. The tablets I mentioned, only when it's bad. And I was told years ago my blood pressure is high, so I take amlodipine, 5 milligrams, every morning.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And my sister keeps posting her biotin gummies, the ones she takes herself for her hair. I've told Mum not to start random things off the internet.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Quite right to leave the biotin alone. Any tummy trouble with the diclofenac tablets?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems. I always have them with a biscuit, so I assumed I was fine.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. Day to day, how are you managing the house?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I live on my own, Lauren's about ten minutes away. I can still cook and that. Gardening is what I miss, I did the pots and the knee complained for two days.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Makes sense. Can I have a look at the knee? I'll be gentle.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. It's the right one. Will it hurt? I tense up, I'm sorry.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me if you want me to stop. It's tender along the inner side of the right knee, and I can't feel a big swelling today. You bend it to about a right angle before it protests, so flexion is limited, but the ligaments feel steady and it's not wobbly.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's not ruined? I was sure you'd say the cartilage had gone.

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely osteoarthritis of the right knee, the wear-and-tear sort. The stairs, the night ache, and what I can feel today all fit. I'm not calling it definite without pictures, but that's my working impression.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Osteoarthritis. That's not cancer, is it? I know that's silly, but people say tumours hide in bones. Could it be?
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): I don't think this is a tumour. The pattern is a joint that's wearing, not something spreading. We don't have to x-ray it today.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. What about my weight, then? If I'm 86.5, is that why the knee's bad? How much do I have to lose, and if I only lose a little is it pointless?

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Weight does load the knee, yes. You don't need a dramatic diet. Even a few kilograms, if it comes off gently, often eases this sort of pain. No crash diets, just walking you can tolerate and smaller portions.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've been saying that. She still has biscuits with her tea, three of them.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Two. Usually two. Don't make me sound worse than I am. If I lose weight will the pain go completely, and what if I can't, because the knee stops me walking?
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): It may ease rather than vanish, and that's still worth having. We can build activity round what the knee allows. Now, those tablets and your stomach.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I said it was fine, but actually, um, I do get heartburn in the evenings. A burning feeling, behind the breastbone. Not every night. I didn't think it counted as a stomach problem.

[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thank you for saying, that does count. I'd like you to pause the diclofenac tablets for now. Keep the gel morning and night, it's fine with amlodipine for your blood pressure. You can use paracetamol as well, one gram up to four times a day from the chemist, for the ache.

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Pause them completely, even twice a week? What if the gel isn't enough at night? Is paracetamol safe with amlodipine? How many tablets is one gram, I don't want to take too many pills.

[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, pause them even twice a week, at least until the heartburn settles. One gram is two 500 milligram tablets. Paracetamol is fine alongside amlodipine. If the night pain is still miserable, that's where the other options come in.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I think I understand. Sorry, I have to write things down or I lose them. Lauren, are you writing?
[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm writing. Gel stays, tablets stop, paracetamol if she needs it.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): The other options are physiotherapy, or a steroid injection into the knee. Either might help. I'm not deciding that today, and you don't have to choose in the corridor.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): An injection, into the knee? Does that hurt? What if it doesn't work, and will physio make me do stairs? Which one is better? What would you do if it was your mum?

[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): The injection is a bit sharp, then it often settles over a day or two. It doesn't work for everyone. Physio is gentler and teaches you stairs without flaring the knee. We'll leave both open, I'm not choosing for you.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): So neither is booked? I just want to be sure I'm not missing a slot. If I do nothing, will the knee collapse?

[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Neither is booked, no. The knee will not collapse because we wait. I'd like to see you again in six weeks, and then we'll choose physio, or the injection, or neither, depending on how you are.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. What if the heartburn gets worse before that, or the knee swells up suddenly? Do I just wait? And can I garden at all, or is that banned?

[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Don't wait if the heartburn is severe, or if the knee suddenly swells, goes hot, or you can't walk on it, phone us or go to urgent care. Light gardening is fine if you pace yourself and stop when it nags. We'll see you in six weeks.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Physiotherapy discussed as an option; no referral was made.

omissions.text: Diclofenac tablet dose is 25 mg, not just unspecified; the patient explicitly said she does not take 50 mg tablets and uses 25 mg tablets only sometimes about twice a week.
The doctor said an X-ray was not needed today ('We don't have to x-ray it today').
Paracetamol dosing instruction was clarified as 1 gram = two 500 mg tablets.
Physiotherapy and steroid injection were discussed but explicitly not booked/decided today; the doctor said neither is booked and the choice would be made at review depending on progress.

omissions.text: Diclofenac tablets were initially listed in the record as 50 mg by the nurse/system list, but the patient explicitly corrected this as wrong and said she takes 25 mg tablets only sometimes; the medication list discrepancy was part of the consultation.
The right knee pain is described as a deep ache inside the knee that wakes her at night two or three nights a week.
Going up stairs is easier than going down stairs.
Right knee puffiness was specified as being worse by the evening on some days.

The patient denied stomach problems when first asked about diclofenac tablets, then corrected herself to report evening heartburn; the initial denial and subsequent revision are not captured as a change/uncertainty in history.
The doctor reassured that diclofenac gel is fine to use with amlodipine for blood pressure.
The doctor advised walking she can tolerate and smaller portions, specifically avoiding crash diets, as part of weight-loss counselling.
The doctor advised that the knee would not collapse if they waited before choosing physiotherapy or injection.

Physiotherapy was described as gentler and aimed at teaching her stairs without flaring the knee; steroid injection was described as a bit sharp and often settling over a day or two, but not working for everyone.
The doctor said he did not think this was a tumour/cancer, explaining the pattern fit a wearing joint rather than something spreading.
